 Social Security Stimulus: Leading Retiree Group Pushing for $1,400 Payment
 The Senior Citizens League is calling on the new Democratic-controlled Congress to pass a one-time $1,400 senior stimulus, citing rising Medicare costs and a COLA that falls short of helping retirees.
 By Leada Gore
al.com
(TNS)
 A leading senior citizens advocacy group is calling on Congress to issue a special one-time stimulus to combat rising inflation and “inadequate” Social Security raise.
 The Senior Citizens League is calling on the new Democratic-controlled Congress to pass a one-time $1,400 senior stimulus, citing rising Medicare costs and the recently passed 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment the group says falls short of helping retirees. The COLA will add roughly $75 a month to the average benefit but that will drop to $65.50 a month after the Medicare increase.
 “Benefits reform can absolutely happen even if two different parties control the Capitol and the White House,” TSCL Executive Director Shannon Benton said in a statement. “Ensuring Americans can retire with dignity isn’t a left-wing issue or a right-wing issue; it’s not a Democratic issue or a Republican issue. It affects all of us, and all of us stand to lose if Congress fails to act to protect America’s seniors.”

 TSCL also called for Congress to restore budget cuts to Medicare and Medicaid from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, add dental, vision and hearing coverage to Medicare and lifting or eliminating the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes.
 Currently, earnings above a certain threshold ($184,500 in 2026, increasing to $192,300 in 2027) are exempt from the Social Security payroll taxes. Lawmakers have looked at eliminating that cap as one way to address the looming Social Security shortfall. Barring congressional action, Social Security will be unable to pay full benefits by late 2032 due to depletion of the reserves for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund. At that point, benefits would be cut by as much as 24%, or roughly $540 a month.
 Benton said while the shortfall is a major issue, there are other more immediate needs as well.
 “While we can’t take Social Security’s looming insolvency out of the spotlight, it’s not a reason to downplay other issues facing retirees. Even without any insolvency-driven benefit cuts, millions of seniors already struggle to pay for food, basic healthcare, and even housing,” she said.
